case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a bankruptcy debtor’s failure to disclose a pending civil claim can be treated as “not inadvertent” (and thus judicially estopped) based only on the debtor’s knowledge and an abstract motive to conceal, or whether courts must instead make a holistic, fact-specific inquiry into intent and overall circumstances consistent with New Hampshire v. Maine.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal common-law doctrine of judicial estoppel as applied in the bankruptcy-disclosure context under the Bankruptcy Code’s disclosure regime (e.g., the debtor’s duty to schedule assets and causes of action under 11 U.S.C. § 521 and related provisions governing property of the estate, including 11 U.S.C. § 541).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Keathley argues the Fifth Circuit misapplied judicial estoppel by using an effectively categorical rule that infers bad faith (i.e., that nondisclosure was not inadvertent) from two factors alone—(1) the debtor’s knowledge of the claim and (2) a theoretical motive to conceal—rather than conducting the equitable, holistic assessment required by New Hampshire v. Maine. He contends this approach is inconsistent with judicial estoppel’s purpose (protecting judicial integrity, not imposing a punitive forfeiture), is overinclusive (sweeping in negligent or mistaken omissions), and improperly harms bankruptcy stakeholders by extinguishing potentially valuable estate assets that could pay creditors. The United States (supporting vacatur) likewise urges a totality-of-circumstances inquiry into inadvertence/bad faith rather than a rigid inference rule.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Buddy Ayers Construction argues judicial estoppel properly bars Keathley’s personal-injury suit because he repeatedly and deliberately omitted the existence of separately pending personal-injury and workers’ compensation claims from his bankruptcy schedules and disclosed them only after the defendant raised nondisclosure in a summary-judgment motion. Respondent defends the Fifth Circuit’s approach as a permissible application of judicial estoppel to protect the integrity of the bankruptcy process and prevent debtors from taking inconsistent positions—telling the bankruptcy court they have no such assets while later seeking recovery in civil litigation—and contends estoppel can apply regardless of direct proof of subjective bad faith when the circumstances show strategic nondisclosure.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas makes the strongest point for affirmance: the repeated omissions, corrected only after a summary-judgment motion, can be compelling, record-based evidence of strategic inconsistency rather than mistake. But that goes to the proper application of New Hampshire v. Maine on a full equitable record, not to the Fifth Circuit’s articulation of a “knowledge + generalized motive” formulation that risks functioning as a near-categorical substitute for the intent-focused inquiry New Hampshire demands. As Justice Kagan and Justice Alito emphasize, motive to conceal in bankruptcy is ubiquitous, and treating it as effectively dispositive risks punishing negligence as fraud while producing a forfeiture that may undermine creditor recoveries. The narrower and more doctrinally faithful disposition is to vacate and remand for a totality-of-circumstances determination of bad faith—without foreclosing that, on these facts, estoppel may ultimately be warranted.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kagan are correct that the Fifth Circuit’s “knowledge + motive” formulation, stated at a high level of generality, can harden into a mechanical proxy that New Hampshire v. Maine cautions against. But our task is to decide this case on the question properly presented and the record actually developed, and here the undisputed sequence—repeated omissions of known claims and correction only after the civil defendant raised nondisclosure in a dispositive motion—supplies record-tethered evidence of strategic inconsistency rather than mere mistake. Even accepting Justice Alito’s point that motive is ubiquitous in bankruptcy, this record contains more than generic motive; it shows a course of conduct that passes directly on the equitable factors New Hampshire identifies, namely inconsistent positions adopted to obtain advantage and threatening the integrity of the bankruptcy process. I would affirm on the narrower ground that, under New Hampshire’s flexible framework as applied to these facts, estoppel is permissible—without endorsing any irrebuttable “knowledge + motive” rule for future cases.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas is correct that the repeated omissions, followed by correction only after a summary-judgment motion, can be powerful evidence that this debtor acted strategically rather than by mistake. But as the Chief Justice notes, the Fifth Circuit’s stated “knowledge + motive” formulation risks converting that probative sequence into a near-presumption, effectively substituting a constructive-knowledge proxy for the actual, record-based intent inquiry New Hampshire v. Maine requires. Because “motive” in bankruptcy is nearly ubiquitous, treating it as dispositive threatens to sweep negligence into bad faith and expands an equitable doctrine beyond its footing. The right course is vacatur and remand for a holistic determination of deliberate manipulation on this record—leaving ample room for estoppel if the facts genuinely show it.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that the record—repeated nondisclosures and amendment only after a summary-judgment motion—can strongly support an inference of strategic inconsistency, and nothing in New Hampshire v. Maine requires a court to ignore that sequence. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, the Fifth Circuit’s articulation risks converting ubiquitous bankruptcy “motive” plus knowledge into a near-dispositive proxy for bad faith, effectively collapsing the intent/mistake distinction New Hampshire builds into its flexible framework. That shortcut is difficult to square with the doctrine’s equitable character and with bankruptcy’s structure, which aims to marshal estate value for creditors rather than create forfeiture windfalls for civil defendants. The appropriate course is to vacate and remand for a totality-of-circumstances inquiry that can still, on these facts, support estoppel if the lower court makes a concrete, record-based finding of manipulation.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that this particular sequence—repeated omissions cured only after the civil defendant raised the nondisclosure—can be compelling evidence of strategic inconsistency, and nothing in New Hampshire v. Maine prevents a court from drawing that inference on a full record. But the Chief Justice correctly identifies the problem with the Fifth Circuit’s articulation: “knowledge + generic motive” is so ubiquitous in bankruptcy that, if treated as dispositive, it risks turning an equitable, intent-focused doctrine into a near-irrebuttable presumption that punishes negligence and confers windfalls on tort defendants at creditors’ expense. The coherent, workable path is vacatur and remand for a totality-of-circumstances inquiry into intent and the actual threat to judicial integrity—one that can still result in estoppel here if the findings show deliberate manipulation. That approach keeps faith with New Hampshire’s flexible framework while avoiding a categorical rule that would distort Chapter 13’s ongoing, lawyer-mediated disclosure regime.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas offers the strongest point for respondent: repeated omissions followed by correction only after a summary-judgment motion can be compelling evidence of strategic inconsistency and may ultimately warrant estoppel under New Hampshire v. Maine. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, the Fifth Circuit’s stated “knowledge + motive” formulation risks hardening an equitable, intent-sensitive doctrine into a near-presumption, because “motive” is ubiquitous in bankruptcy and would sweep negligence into fraud. New Hampshire cautions against mechanical application, and we should not allow judge-made estoppel to expand into a broad forfeiture untethered to a holistic, record-based inquiry—especially where the Bankruptcy Code provides the primary framework for disclosure and administration. Vacatur and remand best respects the equitable nature of the doctrine and separation-of-powers limits while leaving room for estoppel on these facts if the lower courts make the requisite bad-faith findings.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas identifies the strongest point for respondent: the repeated omissions and correction only after a summary-judgment motion are substantial, record-based indicia of strategic inconsistency and may ultimately justify estoppel. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan stress, the question presented is whether the Fifth Circuit may effectively treat “knowledge + generic motive” as dispositive, even though motive is nearly omnipresent in bankruptcy and New Hampshire v. Maine rejects mechanical shortcuts in an equitable doctrine. The proper approach is a tailored, fact-intensive inquiry requiring concrete findings about intent and the threat to judicial integrity, with attention to bankruptcy realities (counsel, trustee actions, amendments, and creditor effects). Vacatur and remand preserves flexibility to reach estoppel on this record while preventing a categorical inference rule that risks punitive forfeiture and a windfall to the civil defendant.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point is that the repeated omissions and the timing of the amendment—only after a summary-judgment motion—are record-based facts that can support an inference of strategic inconsistency and thus estoppel under New Hampshire v. Maine. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that the Fifth Circuit’s articulation risks converting two nearly ubiquitous features of bankruptcy (knowledge of the claim and some incentive to minimize assets) into a near-dispositive rule, which is hard to reconcile with New Hampshire’s insistence that judicial estoppel is an equitable, context-sensitive doctrine. The better course is to reject the categorical formulation and remand for a holistic, record-tethered intent inquiry that may still yield estoppel given the sequence Justice Thomas emphasizes. That preserves flexibility, avoids punishing negligence as fraud by presumption, and keeps the doctrine aligned with its stated purpose of protecting judicial integrity.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right that this record—multiple omissions followed by correction only after a summary-judgment motion—can be potent evidence of strategic inconsistency and may well justify estoppel on remand. But as the Chief Justice emphasizes, the question presented is the Fifth Circuit’s articulation: treating “knowledge + generalized motive” as sufficient to negate inadvertence risks converting an equitable, context-sensitive doctrine under New Hampshire v. Maine into a near-categorical forfeiture rule. That shortcut is especially problematic in bankruptcy, where disclosure is ongoing and lawyer-mediated and where a mechanical presumption can divert value away from creditors and toward a civil defendant, undermining the Bankruptcy Code’s centralized administration aims. Vacatur and remand for a holistic intent inquiry preserves the ability to impose estoppel on these facts while preventing the doctrine’s scope from expanding beyond its equitable foundations.

John Roberts.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is an equitable doctrine whose application turns on a case-specific assessment of whether the party actually adopted inconsistent positions in a way that threatens the integrity of the judicial process, and New Hampshire v. Maine cautions against rigid, mechanical rules. The Fifth Circuit’s approach—treating nondisclosure as “not inadvertent” whenever the debtor knew of the claim and had a generalized motive to conceal—collapses the inquiry into an effectively categorical presumption, sweeping in negligent or mistaken omissions that New Hampshire says should not be punished as fraud. On these facts, Keathley’s repeated nondisclosures are relevant and may ultimately support estoppel, but equity requires courts to examine the full circumstances (including whether he informed counsel, the timing and promptness of amendments, the bankruptcy court’s treatment, and the effect on creditors) rather than inferring bad faith from knowledge plus an abstract motive that exists in virtually every bankruptcy. A rule that strips the inquiry of its functional, fact-bound character risks converting judicial estoppel from a tool to protect judicial integrity into a forfeiture device that can defeat potentially valuable estate assets without the tailored findings New Hampshire contemplates.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under New Hampshire v. Maine, judicial estoppel is an equitable doctrine aimed at preventing a party from prevailing on one position in a court and then later taking an inconsistent position to gain an advantage; the inquiry, though flexible, still must be tethered to the record and the specific elements showing inconsistency and advantage-seeking. Here, Keathley repeatedly omitted pending personal-injury and workers’ compensation claims from his bankruptcy schedules—despite knowing of those claims—and corrected the omission only after the civil defendant raised nondisclosure in a summary-judgment motion, an undisputed sequence of events strongly indicating strategic inconsistency rather than mere mistake. Even if the Fifth Circuit sometimes describes “knowledge + motive” as sufficient, these particular facts satisfy the doctrine’s core concern with protecting the integrity of the bankruptcy process: Keathley represented to the bankruptcy court that he had no such assets while simultaneously pursuing recoveries elsewhere. On this record, the lower court’s application of estoppel does not rest on an abstract, categorical presumption untethered to facts, but on concrete conduct showing an inconsistent litigation position taken to obtain an advantage, so I would affirm.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine treats judicial estoppel as an equitable doctrine calling for a context-sensitive inquiry, not a mechanical rule, and the Fifth Circuit’s “knowledge + theoretical motive” inference effectively collapses the required intent/bad-faith assessment into a constructive-knowledge proxy. That approach resembles treating mere “disclosure-related” facts (here, the debtor’s awareness of the claim and the general incentive to minimize assets in bankruptcy) as dispositive of a more demanding mental-state showing, even though such facts are at most probative and do not themselves establish deliberate manipulation. The categorical inference also lacks a secure doctrinal foundation in this Court’s precedent and expands the doctrine beyond its settled limits by making estoppel turn on abstractions rather than the debtor’s actual intent and the totality of the Chapter 13 circumstances (including the timing and manner of any correction and the role of counsel and the trustee). Because the record as described includes repeated omissions but no individualized finding of strategic deception beyond the inference rule, I would vacate and require the holistic inquiry New Hampshire contemplates.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is an equitable, discretionary doctrine, and New Hampshire v. Maine instructs courts to apply it through a flexible, fact-specific assessment rather than a rigid proxy test. The Fifth Circuit’s near-categorical inference that a nondisclosure was “not inadvertent” whenever the debtor knew of the claim and had a generalized incentive to conceal reads intent out of the inquiry and treats omission as conclusive, even though the Bankruptcy Code’s disclosure regime and the doctrine’s purpose focus on whether the litigant actually sought to manipulate the judicial process. On this record—where nondisclosure is serious but intent may turn on the Chapter 13 context, the debtor’s explanations, the timing and manner of any correction, reliance by the bankruptcy court, and prejudice to creditors—a holistic inquiry is required before imposing the severe remedy of forfeiture. Because the Fifth Circuit’s rule substitutes an abstract motive for the demanded totality-of-circumstances analysis, vacatur and remand for a proper equitable inquiry is warranted.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is an equitable, context-dependent doctrine, and New Hampshire v. Maine rejects mechanical rules in favor of a holistic inquiry focused on whether the later position reflects bad-faith manipulation of the courts. A Fifth Circuit approach that deems nondisclosure “not inadvertent” based only on (1) knowledge of the claim and (2) a generalized motive to conceal effectively collapses the intent inquiry into a near-irrebuttable presumption—one that is overinclusive in a disclosure regime as complex and lawyer-mediated as Chapter 13 and that can perversely reduce recoveries for creditors by wiping out potentially valuable estate assets. On these facts—where nondisclosure is undisputed but the record must still be assessed for intent, correction efforts, trustee involvement, and the bankruptcy court’s response—the proper course is to require a totality-of-circumstances determination rather than impose estoppel categorically. That more workable, coherent rule better serves judicial integrity without turning estoppel into a punitive forfeiture disconnected from the bankruptcy system’s statutory purposes.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is a federal common-law, equitable doctrine, and New Hampshire v. Maine instructs courts to apply it flexibly, attentive to context and without “mechanical” rules that punish “inadvertence or mistake.” The Fifth Circuit’s near-categorical inference that nondisclosure is “not inadvertent” whenever a debtor knew of the claim and had a theoretical motive to conceal collapses the doctrine into a presumption, untethered from the fact-specific inquiry into intent that equity demands and that is especially necessary in the disclosure-heavy, lawyer-and-trustee-driven Chapter 13 setting. Whatever the troubling timing here—Keathley’s correction coming only after summary-judgment pressure—those facts are part of a holistic intent analysis, not a substitute for it, and a rigid inference risks forfeiting estate value to the detriment of creditors contrary to the Bankruptcy Code’s structure. Separation-of-powers principles also counsel against lower courts hardening an equitable, judge-made doctrine into an effectively categorical bar absent direction from Congress or this Court.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine describes judicial estoppel as a flexible, equitable doctrine that turns on context-specific indicia of intentional self-contradiction, not a mechanical presumption. In the bankruptcy-disclosure setting, the Fifth Circuit’s knowledge-plus-abstract-motive inference is effectively categorical because every debtor with a known claim typically has some potential incentive to omit it, so the rule risks sweeping in negligent or mistaken omissions without the concrete, record-based findings of bad faith that equity requires. A holistic inquiry into the debtor’s intent and surrounding circumstances (including the pattern of omissions, whether the debtor alerted counsel, timing and candor of any amendment, and the bankruptcy court’s own view) better protects the integrity of the courts while avoiding the perverse consequence of extinguishing potentially valuable estate assets that could benefit creditors. Here, even if the respondent points to repeated nondisclosure and late disclosure after a summary-judgment motion, the proper course is to require the lower courts to make the requisite fact-specific findings rather than treating knowledge and motive alone as dispositive.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is a federal common-law, equitable doctrine, and New Hampshire v. Maine directs courts to apply it flexibly by considering multiple factors rather than by substituting a mechanical inference rule for a fact-specific assessment. The Fifth Circuit’s approach—treating nondisclosure as “not inadvertent” based solely on knowledge of the claim plus a generic “motive to conceal” that exists in virtually every bankruptcy—reads the intent inquiry out of the analysis and fails to account for the surrounding circumstances (including how and when the omission was corrected and whether the debtor’s conduct actually threatened the integrity of the bankruptcy proceeding). That categorical shortcut is especially problematic on these facts because it risks imposing a punitive forfeiture and conferring a windfall on the civil defendant while potentially diminishing the estate’s value for creditors, a result New Hampshire’s equitable framework does not compel. The proper course is to require a holistic inquiry into whether Keathley’s repeated omissions, timing of correction, and overall conduct demonstrate the kind of bad-faith inconsistency that justifies estoppel, rather than presuming it from two ubiquitous considerations.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine frames judicial estoppel as an equitable, context-dependent doctrine that turns on whether a party’s inconsistent position reflects an effort to mislead a court; that structure resists a mechanical rule that deems nondisclosure “not inadvertent” whenever the debtor knew of the claim and could theoretically benefit. In the bankruptcy setting, the Code’s disclosure regime (§ 521, with estate scope under § 541) is designed to marshal assets for creditors in an orderly, centralized process, and a categorical estoppel rule risks extinguishing estate value based on negligence or confusion rather than intentional manipulation—undermining that system-level purpose. Here, while respondent points to repeated omissions and late correction, the Fifth Circuit’s knowledge-plus-motive inference short-circuits the fact-specific inquiry into intent and surrounding circumstances (including the Chapter 13 context, trustee oversight, amendments, and what the bankruptcy court did once the omission surfaced) that New Hampshire demands. Proper application requires vacatur and a remand for a holistic intent analysis rather than treating abstract motive as a substitute for proof of bad faith in this record.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a bankruptcy debtor’s failure to disclose a pending civil claim can be treated as “not inadvertent” for judicial-estoppel purposes based only on the debtor’s knowledge of the claim and a motive to conceal, or instead requires a holistic, fact-specific inquiry into intent and surrounding circumstances consistent with New Hampshire v. Maine.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Equitable doctrine of judicial estoppel (federal common law) as applied in the bankruptcy-disclosure context under the Bankruptcy Code’s disclosure regime (e.g., debtor schedules and statements requiring disclosure of assets/claims).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Keathley argues the Fifth Circuit applied an overly rigid, effectively per se judicial-estoppel rule that infers bad faith (i.e., that nondisclosure was “not inadvertent”) merely from (1) the debtor’s knowledge of the underlying facts/claim and (2) a potential motive to conceal. Petitioner contends this approach conflicts with New Hampshire v. Maine’s equitable, discretionary framework requiring courts to evaluate all relevant circumstances. He maintains that judicial estoppel should not automatically bar a personal-injury claim when bankruptcy omissions occur, especially where the bankruptcy system has tools to address nondisclosure (amendment, trustee administration, creditor payment) and where a mechanical estoppel rule can unjustly shift the windfall to the tort defendant rather than protecting creditors or the bankruptcy court’s integrity.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Buddy Ayers Construction argues judicial estoppel may properly bar a plaintiff from pursuing an undisclosed civil claim when the plaintiff took inconsistent positions in bankruptcy (omitting the asset) and later in litigation (asserting it), and that the doctrine can be applied without requiring direct evidence of subjective bad faith. Respondent emphasizes that Keathley deliberately and repeatedly omitted the pending personal-injury and workers’ compensation claims from bankruptcy schedules and disclosed them only after the defendant moved for summary judgment based on the omission, supporting estoppel to protect judicial integrity and deter strategic nondisclosure. Respondent defends the Fifth Circuit’s inference-based approach as administrable and consistent with the doctrine’s purpose.

John Roberts.reasoning: Respondent’s strongest point is administrability and protecting the integrity of the bankruptcy process: because disclosure is central, knowledge of the claim plus an incentive to conceal will often indicate bad faith. But as Justice Kagan emphasizes, New Hampshire v. Maine rejects “inflexible prerequisites,” and the Fifth Circuit’s knowledge-plus-motive approach functions as just such a rigid rule—treating two commonly present facts as dispositive and foreclosing contrary evidence on intent. Consistent with Justice Thomas’s focus on contemporaneous intent, the equitable inquiry should remain circumstance-sensitive: knowledge and motive are highly probative, but cannot by rule establish lack of “inadvertence or mistake,” especially where the Code provides corrective mechanisms that can protect creditors without awarding a windfall to a civil defendant. Vacatur and remand for a holistic, totality-of-the-circumstances intent inquiry is therefore the proper, narrow disposition.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Respondent’s strongest point is that bankruptcy’s disclosure regime is foundational and that repeated omissions, corrected only after dispositive motions, strongly suggest manipulation. But as the Chief Justice explains, New Hampshire v. Maine rejects rigid prerequisites, and the Fifth Circuit’s knowledge-plus-motive approach hardens a flexible equitable doctrine into a near-conclusive presumption untethered to the debtor’s contemporaneous, subjective intent at the time the schedules were filed and amended. That move effectively collapses an intent inquiry into mere knowledge plus an abstract incentive—conditions present in virtually every nondisclosure case—and risks awarding a windfall to the civil defendant rather than protecting the estate through bankruptcy’s own mechanisms, as Justice Kagan notes. Vacatur and remand are therefore appropriate so the lower court can evaluate the full record of intent under a totality-of-the-circumstances framework.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Respondent’s strongest point—emphasized in various ways by several colleagues—is that bankruptcy depends on complete disclosure and that a knowledge-plus-motive rule is administrable and protective of the court’s integrity. But as Chief Justice Roberts explains, New Hampshire v. Maine rejects inflexible formulations for an equitable doctrine, and the Fifth Circuit’s approach effectively converts two probative circumstances into a dispositive presumption that displaces the required inquiry into actual intent. Knowledge and motive are certainly relevant evidence from which a court may infer bad faith, but they do not themselves satisfy the ultimate element; a debtor may know of a claim and have a generic incentive yet still omit it through mistake, confusion, or reliance on counsel—facts that must remain legally cognizable. I therefore agree with Justice Thomas that we should vacate and remand for a holistic, circumstance-sensitive assessment rather than an atextual expansion of the standard into near-constructive intent.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Respondent’s strongest point is administrability and the need to protect the integrity of the bankruptcy process given a debtor’s affirmative duty of full disclosure—especially where omissions are repeated and corrected only after a dispositive motion. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, New Hampshire v. Maine frames judicial estoppel as an equitable doctrine that rejects “inflexible prerequisites,” and the Fifth Circuit’s knowledge-plus-motive test effectively converts two probative facts into a dispositive presumption of bad faith. That shortcut risks producing unfair, anomalous results by awarding a windfall to the civil defendant while bypassing bankruptcy’s own corrective mechanisms that can protect the estate and creditors, a concern Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch both underscore. Those timing and repetition facts remain powerful evidence on remand, but they cannot be treated as conclusive by rule where equity demands consideration of all the circumstances bearing on intent.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Respondent’s strongest point remains that bankruptcy’s disclosure regime depends on candor, and repeated omissions corrected only after a dispositive motion can be powerful evidence of strategic concealment. But as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, New Hampshire v. Maine rejects “inflexible prerequisites,” and the Fifth Circuit’s knowledge-plus-motive formulation functions as a dispositive rule in a setting where those factors are nearly always present. Justice Barrett’s windfall concern underscores the structural mismatch: the Bankruptcy Code supplies tools—amendment, trustee control, and bankruptcy-court sanctions—to protect creditors and the court without automatically forfeiting the claim to the civil defendant. Vacatur and remand best honors the equitable, context-sensitive inquiry our precedent requires, while leaving ample room for estoppel if the full record shows intent to mislead.

The right course is vacatur and remand for a totality, intent-focused inquiry where repeated omissions and late correction can carry great weight without being treated as dispositive by rule.

The better fit with the established content of judicial estoppel—and with the Bankruptcy Code’s own remedial machinery—is to treat knowledge and motive as powerful evidence while still allowing consideration of contrary facts bearing on inadvertence or mistake. Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Respondent’s strongest point is that bankruptcy’s disclosure regime is foundational, and a strong knowledge-plus-motive inference may deter concealment and protect the bankruptcy court’s integrity. Maine rejects turning probative factors into an “inflexible” rule, and the Fifth Circuit’s approach effectively makes knowledge and a generic incentive dispositive in a way that displaces the equitable, intent-focused inquiry. The Bankruptcy Code’s structure already embeds targeted checks—amendments, trustee control of estate property, and bankruptcy-court sanctions—so importing a near-per-se presumption risks expanding estoppel beyond what is necessary and, as Justice Kagan notes, can divert value from creditors to a civil defendant windfall. The better course is vacatur and remand for a holistic assessment in which knowledge, motive, timing, and repetition remain powerful evidence but not a categorical substitute for actual intent.

John Roberts.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine supplies the governing framework, and it treats judicial estoppel as a flexible, equitable doctrine guided by several factors rather than a rigid rule—so a circuit rule deeming nondisclosure “not inadvertent” based solely on knowledge plus a generic motive effectively adds an extra, court-made threshold that New Hampshire does not require. Looking to substance over labels, the question is the debtor’s actual intent in the bankruptcy process: whether the omission was a strategic effort to mislead the bankruptcy court, or instead an error that can be addressed within the Code’s disclosure-and-amendment regime and trustee administration without forfeiting the civil claim. A per se inference risks making the equitable doctrine incompatible with the Bankruptcy Code’s structure by shifting value away from the estate and creditors and handing a windfall to the tort defendant, even when the omission can be cured and the bankruptcy court’s integrity protected by less drastic measures. Consistent with New Hampshire’s totality-of-circumstances approach, the case should require a holistic, fact-specific inquiry into intent and surrounding circumstances rather than treating knowledge and motive as dispositive.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is an equitable, judge-made doctrine, and New Hampshire v. Maine makes clear it is not governed by a rigid checklist but by a fact-specific assessment of whether a party is abusing the judicial process. The Fifth Circuit’s rule effectively treats nondisclosure as “not inadvertent” whenever the debtor knew of the claim and had any motive to conceal, collapsing the requisite culpable state of mind into a near-per-se inference untethered from what the debtor actually believed and intended when filing the schedules. On these facts—where the estoppel determination turns on the debtor’s mental state at the time of the bankruptcy filings and later amendments—a court must examine the surrounding circumstances and contemporaneous intent rather than presume deception from knowledge plus generalized incentive. Because the court below treated that inference as dispositive and left no room for contrary evidence bearing on intent, the judgment should be vacated for application of the proper, holistic standard.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine describes judicial estoppel as an equitable, discretionary doctrine and expressly rejects any “inflexible” or “general formulation,” which makes the Fifth Circuit’s near-per-se inference (knowledge of the claim + motive to conceal = not inadvertent) doctrinally suspect. Knowledge and potential motive are certainly evidence relevant to intent, but they do not themselves satisfy the ultimate intent inquiry; treating them as automatically dispositive improperly collapses probative circumstances into an element-like rule. On this record—where the debtor’s omission is serious and repeated—the proper course is still a holistic assessment of surrounding circumstances (including explanations, timing of correction, trustee/creditor effects, and whether the bankruptcy court was actually misled) rather than a categorical shortcut. Fidelity to the governing standard as articulated by this Court requires rejecting an atextual, judge-made presumption that displaces equitable discretion and fact-specific intent analysis.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is an equitable, discretionary doctrine, and New Hampshire v. Maine instructs courts to weigh all relevant circumstances rather than adopt rigid, atextual shortcuts for inferring intent. The Fifth Circuit’s knowledge-plus-motive test effectively functions as a near per se rule that treats nondisclosure as “not inadvertent” without engaging the holistic inquiry equity requires—especially in bankruptcy, where omissions may stem from confusion, attorney error, or subsequent correction, and where the Code provides mechanisms (amendment, trustee administration) to protect creditors without gifting a windfall to the tort defendant. On these facts—where the estoppel ruling turns primarily on inference from Keathley’s awareness of the claim and generalized incentive to conceal—equitable principles demand a fact-specific assessment of intent and surrounding circumstances, including the timing and explanation for any corrections, rather than categorical estoppel. Because the court below truncated that inquiry, I would vacate and remand for application of the full New Hampshire framework to the particular record here.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under well-settled precedent, New Hampshire v. Maine treats judicial estoppel as an equitable, discretionary doctrine that turns on context—including whether the prior position resulted from “inadvertence or mistake”—not a near-conclusive presumption drawn from two generic facts. The Fifth Circuit’s approach, which deems nondisclosure “not inadvertent” based essentially on the debtor’s knowledge of the claim and a theoretical motive to conceal, is a contrived shortcut that collapses New Hampshire’s fact-specific inquiry into an effectively per se rule, especially where (as here) bankruptcy law supplies operational mechanisms (amendment, trustee administration, creditor distribution) that can remedy omissions without gifting a windfall to the tort defendant. Given the record’s emphasis on repeated omissions and late disclosure only after a summary-judgment motion, those facts may support estoppel after a holistic inquiry—but they cannot justify a categorical inference that intent is “almost always” established whenever knowledge and motive exist. The judgment should be vacated so courts apply New Hampshire’s totality-of-circumstances framework to these particular nondisclosures rather than an automatic presumption.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine teaches that judicial estoppel is an equitable, discretionary doctrine aimed at deterring “intentional self-contradiction,” and it cautions against applying it where the earlier position resulted from “inadvertence or mistake.” The Fifth Circuit’s near per se rule—treating nondisclosure as “not inadvertent” whenever the debtor knew of the claim and could hypothesize a motive to conceal—collapses that equitable inquiry into an administrable shortcut that risks converting ambiguous silence in schedules into a conclusive, bad-faith representation in every case. That approach also sits uneasily with bankruptcy’s basic structure: the Code already polices nondisclosure (through amendment, trustee administration of estate property, and remedies for dishonesty), and a mechanical estoppel rule can hand a windfall to the tort defendant without materially advancing the creditors’ recovery or the court’s integrity in a case-specific way. On these facts—where estoppel was triggered largely by the omission itself and an inferred motive rather than a holistic examination of surrounding circumstances and intent—the better course is to require the fact-bound New Hampshire inquiry rather than a categorical inference.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: New Hampshire v. Maine describes judicial estoppel as an equitable, discretionary doctrine that turns on context and is not to be applied through a rigid, effectively per se rule. In the bankruptcy-disclosure setting, the Fifth Circuit’s knowledge-plus-motive inference risks collapsing the required intent inquiry into a mechanical presumption, even though the Bankruptcy Code’s disclosure regime and bankruptcy practice provide flexible tools (amendment of schedules, trustee administration, and distribution to creditors) that often better protect the estate and equitable distribution than handing a windfall to a tort defendant. A holistic, fact-specific inquiry—asking whether the omission was actually strategic in light of the record, the timing and explanation for any corrections, and the impact on creditors and the bankruptcy court—better fits the doctrine’s equitable roots and preserves system-level fairness and administrability in multi-party bankruptcy proceedings. On this record, the proper rule is not the Fifth Circuit’s categorical inference, but a totality-of-the-circumstances assessment of intent consistent with longstanding bankruptcy practice and New Hampshire’s framework.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is an equitable doctrine aimed at protecting the integrity of the judicial process by preventing deliberate position-shifting, and New Hampshire v. Maine frames its application as a discretionary, circumstance-sensitive inquiry rather than a mechanical rule. The Fifth Circuit’s approach—treating nondisclosure as “not inadvertent” based solely on the debtor’s knowledge of the claim and a generic motive to conceal—functions as a near-per-se presumption of bad faith, which is difficult to square with equity’s traditional insistence on intent and context. On these facts, Keathley’s repeated omissions are powerful evidence that may ultimately support estoppel, but the doctrine as established requires courts to consider surrounding circumstances (including explanations for the omission and subsequent corrective actions) rather than deeming such evidence irrelevant by rule. The proper course is to reject the rigid inference standard and require a holistic intent inquiry on remand, consistent with the established content and limits of the equitable doctrine.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Judicial estoppel is an equitable doctrine, and New Hampshire v. Maine instructs courts to apply it flexibly by considering all relevant circumstances, not by adopting a categorical inference of bad faith. In the bankruptcy-disclosure setting, the Code’s disclosure regime supplies structured mechanisms—amendment of schedules, trustee administration of assets, and plan/discharge consequences—that already cabin and remedy nondisclosure, so a per se “knowledge + motive” rule risks expanding estoppel beyond what the equitable doctrine’s text and structure (as articulated in our precedents) support. Applying a holistic inquiry here matters because the Fifth Circuit’s approach treats “not inadvertent” as essentially satisfied whenever a debtor knows of a claim and might benefit from omission, instead of asking the fact-specific question New Hampshire demands: whether the debtor acted with the kind of culpable intent that makes estoppel necessary to protect judicial integrity. On these facts—where the omission was later corrected only after a summary-judgment motion—a court may still find estoppel warranted, but it must do so after evaluating intent and surrounding circumstances rather than presuming it from knowledge and generalized motive.
